introduction: Before the First World War ‘Abdu’l-Bahá told audiences in Europe and America that the continent was an arsenal awaiting a spark, and that peace was “the most preventable accident” undone. These passages give the whole of the teaching he was carrying: Bahá’u’lláh’s call to the kings to meet and bind themselves, a tribunal of the nations, a common language, the education of children, the part of women, the hope placed in America, and under all of it the claim that peace is a matter of religion and begins between two people. A hundred of the guide’s 277 quotations are given here, ten from each tenth of its length. Beside them stand a hundred voices from elsewhere: Isaiah and Micah, the Qur’an, the Great Learning, Ashoka, Augustine, Tennyson, Hugo, Whitman, Longfellow, Wilson, the charters written after each war. About one in four doubts the hope or its means and ends in a question: Thucydides, Tacitus, Clausewitz and Heraclitus on what war is, Kant and Madison on what holds a peace, Jefferson on alliances, Yeats in 1919, Hector praying over his son.
questions: “War is the most preventable accident.” Clausewitz called it policy by other means, and the Athenians said the strong do what they can. If they are right about what war is, what would preventing it take?

The readings begin peace between individuals and end with a tribunal of nations. Kant began from the other end, with law. Which has done more for the peace you have known, and do they need each other?
‘Abdu’l-Bahá expected that peoples would refuse the wars their governments wanted, and that mothers would not give their sons. What happened in 1914, and what would make the expectation come true?
A common language is called necessary to peace. Goethe and the story of Babel raise doubts. What can a shared language do, and what can it not?
America is named the standard-bearer of peace. Read Washington, Jefferson, Lincoln and Kipling’s “Recessional” beside that hope. What would a nation have to be to carry such a standard?
Bahá’u’lláh names one common Faith as the sovereign remedy; Madison trusted a multiplicity of sects. What kind of unity would end war without ending freedom?

outside.why: “Peace must first be established among individuals, until it leadeth in the end to peace among nations.” The Confucian Great Learning: persons cultivated, families regulated, states rightly governed, the whole kingdom tranquil.
Peace begins between persons. James asks where wars come from and answers: come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá builds peace upward from love between individuals. Kant thought nations could be held to peace by law and mutual interest even if men were no better than they are. Which way does the building go?
All governments must turn their battleships “to a mighty fleet of merchant marine”. Isaiah’s version: they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks.
Fleets of commerce uniting distant shores. Tennyson saw both futures in one vision: the heavens filled with commerce, and airy navies grappling in the central blue.
Bahá’u’lláh bore all this “that conflict and aggression might be put to flight”. The angels’ song at another birth: on earth peace, good will toward men.

“The greatest intelligence of man is being expended in the direction of killing his fellow-man.” Longfellow, in an arsenal: were half the power that fills the world with terror given to redeem the human mind from error.
“War is the most preventable accident.” Clausewitz did not think it an accident at all: war is a mere continuation of policy by other means. If he is right, what would preventing it require?

The sovereigns are to hold to peace together, and if one takes up arms, all must arise against him. The Qur’an gave believers the same rule: make peace between them, and if one party doeth wrong, fight that which doeth wrong till it return.

Bahá’u’lláh calls the kings to an assembly that will bind the strong. The Athenians told the Melians how the world goes: the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must. What has ever made the strong accept a common rule?
They must “establish a Union of the nations of the world” by a binding treaty. An American president proposed it in 1918: a general association of nations under specific covenants.
The cause of peace is to be “the object of general consultation”. The last hymn of the Rig Veda: assemble, speak together; let your minds be all of one accord.
The League of Nations exists, “yet it is incapable of establishing universal peace”. Jeremiah on healers of his day: saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace.
A Supreme Tribunal with members from every nation. Tennyson’s phrase for it, seventy years earlier: the Parliament of man, the Federation of the world.

Americans can best serve by helping to apply their own federal principle to the world. Jefferson’s first advice to the federation was the opposite: honest friendship with all nations, entangling alliances with none. When did the older counsel stop being wise?

“The true duty of a powerful king is to establish a universal peace.” A British chieftain in Tacitus on the peace a powerful empire brought: they make a solitude and call it peace. How is a universal peace to differ from that one?
“The German will say to the Frenchman, ‘I am a Frenchman.’” Mark Twain on how such feeling is learned: travel is fatal to prejudice, bigotry and narrow-mindedness.
If governments want war “the people will not agree to it”. In 1914 the peoples agreed readily, and Wilfred Owen wrote the anthem for what followed. What would make that refusal real?
A tabernacle through which “the various nations of the earth shall become unified”. Isaiah: mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people.

The sovereign remedy is “one universal Cause, one common Faith”. Madison trusted peace and liberty to a multiplicity of sects and interests, none able to dominate. Is unity of belief the cure for conflict, or one of its old causes?
“The body of the human world is sick … Its life is the Most Great Peace.” Isaiah’s names for the healer he awaited end with this one: the Prince of Peace.
Bahá’u’lláh announced “reconciliation between the religions of the world” as part of peace. Ashoka, after his wars, had it carved in rock: whoever condemns other religions harms his own.
“Quench ye the fires of war, lift high the banners of peace.” Jesus: blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God.

“Religion is the channel of love unto all peoples.” Jesus also said: think not that I am come to send peace on earth: I came not to send peace, but a sword. What kind of division does a religion of love still bring?
The desire for peace “is a matter of religious belief”. The Psalm joins them: mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed each other.
The cause of peace is the Cause of God, “and all the forces of the world are opposed to it”. The Psalmist: I am for peace: but when I speak, they are for war.

Governments “consider militarism as the step to human progress”. A Greek philosopher said so at the beginning: war is the father of all and the king of all. Has anything good come by war that could not have come another way?
“Close your eyes to racial differences, and welcome all with the light of oneness.” Paul: there is neither Jew nor Greek, bond nor free.

Bahá’u’lláh says to close one’s eyes to racial differences. An American judge in 1978: in order to get beyond racism, we must first take account of race. When does not seeing difference heal, and when does it hide a wound?
“The lights of peace and reconciliation dawned forth from the Sun of Truth.” Isaiah: out of Zion shall go forth the law, and all nations shall flow unto it.
“Now it is the beginning of dawn, a little light has appeared.” Jesus: ye can discern the face of the sky; but can ye not discern the signs of the times?
No one imagined the banner of universal peace would be raised, and now the world’s great ones strive for it. Victor Hugo, to a peace congress in 1849: a day will come.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes that “the dawn of peace and reconciliation has broken”. Yeats, in 1919: things fall apart; the centre cannot hold; mere anarchy is loosed upon the world. Which of them read the hour rightly, and over what span of time?
What the Supreme Pen has promised will come, though “humanity as a whole is not yet ready”. Habakkuk: though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come.

“It is most difficult for mothers to send to the battlefield those upon whom they have lavished such love and care.” Julia Ward Howe’s appeal to women in 1870: our sons shall not be taken from us to unlearn all that we have been able to teach them.
“Universal peace is impossible without universal suffrage.” The demand for that suffrage was first made in America in 1848.

Mothers will not send their sons to war. Hector, holding his infant son, prays that the boy will come home from battle with bloody spoils and delight his mother’s heart. How deep does the old honour run, in mothers too?
“Take hold of the viol of love, raise the melody of the Kingdom.” The Psalm: O sing unto the Lord a new song.
The Most Great Peace cannot be organized “unless the unity of languages is realized”. Zamenhof made a language to that end.
One language is wanted for one humanity. In Genesis the world had one language, built a tower, and was scattered. What does that story fear, and does the fear apply?
Misunderstanding will end with a common tongue. Goethe: a man who has no acquaintance with foreign languages knows nothing of his own. What would be lost if all learned one and no other?
“Strong and weak, rich and poor, contending kindreds and hostile nations” will dwell together. Isaiah: the wolf shall dwell with the lamb.
The earth one homeland, the human race one people. The Chinese Book of Rites remembers such an age: a public and common spirit ruled all under the sky.

The five continents become as one. The Tao Te Ching’s ideal is a little state with a small population, its people content never to visit the neighbouring one within earshot. Is a world made one a world made better?
The Word of God “unified opposite types and conflicting elements of human society”. Paul: he is our peace, who hath broken down the middle wall of partition.

“The leaders of religions must be the means of binding the hearts together.” Pascal on what they have often been: men never do evil so completely and cheerfully as when they do it from religious conviction. What has to change in the leaders?
Bahá’ís “consider the earth as one country”. Diogenes, asked his city: I am a citizen of the world.
Qualities and conduct “admired by all peoples” proclaim the oneness of humanity. Jesus: by their fruits ye shall know them.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá longs to read in the newspapers that these people are truthful, trustworthy and kind to all. Jesus: let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works.
“The continent of Europe hath virtually become an arsenal filled with explosives.” Jesus: ye shall hear of wars and rumours of wars.
Three years before the war he warned that “a single flame will set on fire the whole of that continent”. Ezekiel on the watchman’s duty: if he see the sword come, and blow not the trumpet.

“For thousands of years men and nations have gone forth to the battlefield to settle their differences.” Hardy’s soldier on the man he shot: you shoot a fellow down you’d treat if met where any bar is.
If the American republics agreed on peace, Europe might follow. The Qur’an’s rule for an adversary’s first move: if they incline to peace, incline thou also to it.
“This peace will come about after great upheavals.” After two such wars an American general and president counted the cost of preparing for a third.

“Wait! till the end of the war. The New Ideals of Peace … will be promoted.” After the second war the nations wrote: since wars begin in the minds of men, it is in the minds of men that the defences of peace must be constructed.
Bahá’u’lláh wrote of the Most Great Peace “to all the kings and rulers of nations”. Jesus over Jerusalem: if thou hadst known the things which belong unto thy peace.
“Kings could not withstand Him. They endeavored to extinguish His light but served only to increase its intensity.” Gamaliel: if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it.
He wrote to Victoria, the Czar, the Kaiser and Napoleon III. Shelley on what becomes of a king of kings.
“My supreme desire is the unity of the East and West.” Kipling’s ballad: there is neither East nor West, Border, nor Breed, nor Birth.
For this object He “hath again and again been cast into prison”. Lovelace: stone walls do not a prison make.

“This American democracy manifests capacity … to become the standard-bearer of the Most Great Peace.” Washington’s parting counsel: observe good faith and justice towards all nations; cultivate peace and harmony with all.
May the American people and government unite for peace. Lincoln’s last inaugural: to do all which may achieve a just and lasting peace among ourselves and with all nations.

“America is a noble nation, the standard-bearer of peace throughout the world.” Kipling to another great power at its height: lest we forget. What does a nation told such things about itself need to hear as well?
America is to bestow “happiness and prosperity upon the children of men”. The lines on the Statue of Liberty.
“Having heard of the numerous organizations for peace and arbitration … I have come here.” Jesus of others doing good work: he that is not against us is on our part.
Asked the aims of the Cause, he lists oneness, peace, love and cooperation. Micah, asked what the Lord requires: do justly, love mercy, walk humbly.
To a member of Congress: “so must you expend your energy for the benefit of all the nations of the world.” Garrison’s masthead: our country is the world.

A legislator is asked to serve all nations as he serves his own. Burke: to love the little platoon we belong to is the first link in the series by which we proceed towards a love of mankind. Can the last link be reached without the first?

Senators who gave their energies to peace would be listened to. Plato held that cities will have no rest from their evils until philosophers are kings. What do rulers lack that the reading hopes they will find?

“How much better … if these emperors, Kings, Ministers … treated each other according to the law of love.” Machiavelli told princes that it is much safer to be feared than loved. Why have rulers found his advice the easier to follow?

Peace is the best remedy for a people that “cannot withstand the military aggression” of stronger nations. Augustine: peace should be the object of your desire; war should be waged only as a necessity.

Mothers, teachers and professors must plant the thought of universal peace in every student. Moses on how a people’s deepest words are taught: diligently unto thy children, when thou sittest in thine house.

In the college where he studies, a student is to unfurl “the standard of universal peace”. Tagore’s prayer for his country: where the world has not been broken up into fragments by narrow domestic walls.
“It is for us to consider how we may educate men.” Dewey: education is a process of living and not a preparation for future living.
In earlier ages people “could not meet each other”; now the means of unity exist. Whitman on the cable, the canal and the railway: the lands to be welded together.
The means for the unity of mankind are now found. Marx saw what the same means dissolve: all that is solid melts into air. Have faster communications brought the unity expected of them?
“This reformation and tranquility shall not appear except through unity and harmony.” Isaiah: the work of righteousness shall be peace.
May “the people of the world … embrace one another”. Whitman after a civil war: beautiful that war and all its deeds of carnage must in time be utterly lost.
“We must make every deprived one prosperous and every hopeless one hopeful.” Proverbs: plead the cause of the poor and needy.
“Peace and fellowship are factors of upbuilding … war and strife are the causes of destruction.” Augustine’s definition: the peace of all things is the tranquillity of order.
War disintegrates. The Tao Te Ching: arms, however beautiful, are instruments of evil omen.
“The Sun of Truth shines on all alike.” Jesus: he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good.
East and West “will embrace each other”. Schiller’s ode, now the anthem of a continent that fought itself for centuries: all mankind are brethren.
“May [we] arise with the greatest power to serve this most important cause.” Paul: we are labourers together with God.
“Today the courageous one … becomes the cause of illumination.” Joshua: be strong and of a good courage.

The teachings are “the peace of heart and soul” and also the peace of peoples. Jesus distinguishes: my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth. Is inner peace a different thing from peace between nations, or its root?
‘Abdu’l-Bahá quotes this verse of the Qur’an and reads its light as the light of unity.
What causes the unity of the world has flowed from the Pen. The Dhammapada on what does not: victory breeds hatred, for the conquered is unhappy.
“The time has come when all mankind shall be united.” An American president in 1963: our most basic common link is that we all inhabit this small planet.
The Convention “freeth the souls from religious, racial and worldly prejudices”. Peter: God is no respecter of persons.

“Universal peace will be realized and people will become angelic.” Kant held that nothing quite straight can be made from such crooked material as man, and still drew up articles for a perpetual peace. Does peace wait on people becoming angelic?
The Occident is “less fettered by vain imaginings and imitations”. Paul: prove all things; hold fast that which is good.

“This tabernacle of the unity of the human world casts its shade upon all.” The Great Law of the Haudenosaunee: a tree of peace whose roots spread to the four directions, for any nation to trace and shelter under.
Universal peace is named a “sign of the maturity of the world”. Paul: when I became a man, I put away childish things.
Here “the foundation of the wondrous Divine Order will be established”. The nations’ own first article, in 1948: all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.
May all “come together … beneath the shade of the pavilion of the oneness of humanity”. The Psalm: how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity.
“He seeks universal peace and desires the welfare of all.” The Qur’an: God summoneth to the abode of peace.
The hope to serve universal peace “is acceptable at the Threshold of the Almighty”. The Psalm: he maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow.

When the sea of love is set in motion, “new results will appear every hour”. Ashoka, after the slaughter in Kalinga, resolved that even those who do wrong should be forgiven where forgiveness is possible.

“The paradise which is to come on earth, when all mankind will be gathered together under the tent of unity.” Micah: they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree; and none shall make them afraid.

isaiah-work-of-righteousness.text: And the work of righteousness shall be peace; and the effect of righteousness quietness and assurance for ever

psalm-maketh-wars-to-cease.text: He maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder; he burneth the chariot in the fire. Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth

psalm-righteousness-and-peace-have-kisse.text: Mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed each other

jeremiah-peace-when-there-is-no-peace.text: They have healed also the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace

matthew-wars-and-rumours.text: And ye shall hear of wars and rumours of wars: see that ye be not troubled: for all these things must come to pass, but the end is not yet. For nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom: and there shall be famines, and pestilences, and earthquakes, in divers places. All these are the beginning of sorrows

luke-on-earth-peace.text: And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God, and saying, Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men

john-my-peace-i-give.text: Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid

james-whence-come-wars.text: From whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members? Ye lust, and have not: ye kill, and desire to have, and cannot obtain: ye fight and war, yet ye have not, because ye ask not

isaiah-swords-into-plowshares.text: And he shall judge among the nations, and shall rebuke many people: and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more

quran-incline-to-peace.text: And if they incline to peace, incline thou also to it, and trust in Allah. Lo! He, even He, is the Hearer, the Knower.

quran-make-peace-between-them.text: And if two parties of believers fall to fighting, then make peace between them. And if one party of them doeth wrong to the other, fight ye that which doeth wrong till it return unto the ordinance of Allah; then, if it return, make peace between them justly, and act equitably. Lo! Allah loveth the equitable.

quran-abode-of-peace.text: And Allah summoneth to the abode of peace, and leadeth whom He will to a straight path.

dhammapada-victory-breeds-hatred.text: Victory breeds hatred, for the conquered is unhappy. He who has given up both victory and defeat

whitman-reconciliation.text: Word over all, beautiful as the sky, / Beautiful that war and all its deeds of carnage must in time be utterly lost, / That the hands of the sisters Death and Night incessantly softly wash again, and ever again, this soil'd world
whitman-reconciliation.author: Walt Whitman

hardy-quaint-and-curious.text: Yes; quaint and curious war is! / You shoot a fellow down / You'd treat if met where any bar is, / Or help to half-a-crown
hardy-quaint-and-curious.author: Thomas Hardy

washington-good-faith-toward-all-nations.text: Observe good faith and justice towards all Nations; cultivate peace and harmony with all

wilson-association-of-nations.text: A general association of nations must be formed under specific covenants for the purpose of affording mutual guarantees of political independence and territorial integrity to great and small states alike

tacitus-call-it-peace.text: To robbery, slaughter, plunder, they give the lying name of empire; they make a solitude and call it peace
tacitus-call-it-peace.author: Tacitus

thucydides-strong-do-what-they-can.text: since you know as well as we do that right, as the world goes, is only in question between equals in power, while the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must
thucydides-strong-do-what-they-can.author: Thucydides

howe-our-sons-shall-not-be-taken.text: Our sons shall not be taken from us to unlearn All that we have been able to teach them of charity, mercy and patience

tao-instruments-of-evil-omen.text: Now arms, however beautiful, are instruments of evil omen, hateful, it may be said, to all creatures

longfellow-arsenal.text: Were half the power, that fills the world with terror, / Were half the wealth, bestowed on camps and courts, / Given to redeem the human mind from error, / There were no need of arsenals nor forts
